The promise of AI is currently framed as relieving humans of the tedious tasks that encompass work, allowing them to focus on the more rewarding and creative problems of novel discovery and idea generation.

This has been mostly true, but as AI gets better I think it has a high likelihood of becoming a comforting lie that we tell ourselves. The more capable AI becomes, the more humanity will have to resist being relegated to the middle management layer of its own progress. And the larger the risk that all human work becomes machine-like without any real sense of fulfillment or accomplishment. 

As AI gets better at the stuff that goes beyond execution and into the realm of judgement, creativity and purpose, the boundary between AI work and Human Work is going to destabilize. Without a conscious effort to push back against this, it’s easy to see a future where humans are relegated to supervising systems they no longer fully understand. 

“Drudgery” is defined by repitive, tedious tasks. But perhaps a better definition for it would be work with the absence of agency, and under that definition AI can certainly create more of it. Plenty of coders have already experienced a loss of meaning in their work as AI “solves” coding. 

“What is joy without despair” is accepted to be a fair question. But what is self-actualization without the overcoming of friction or frustration. I do worry a bit for the future generations that may live an entire life without experiencing the qualia of success after repeated full-effort attempts met with failure. 

If AI can execute our ideas, it’s likely that eventually it will be able to create better ones. Mastery and ownership of a creation being things of the past is hard to imagine. 

The most valid pushback to this concern is that people still play chess despite engines existing, make furniture from hand regardless of IKEA etc. 

I wonder if we’ll see an investment theme over the next decade that has to do with the “meaning economy”, or whatever people buy when their work is no longer their identity. 

Maybe in the more near term, there’s a trade in the value of accountability. If the vast majority of work isn’t done by a human, who do you yell at / fire when the work is bad? Anyone selling the right to blame a human or to outsource accountability (maybe E&O insurers?) could benefit.

Back in the day I spent thousands of hours getting good at inserting IV caths, I could drop an 18g in a hypovolemic patient with an active hemorrhage in the back of a van going 60mph through traffic. Did it pay me any more to be good at that? No, but it gave me a sense of pride.

What separates useful AI work from ordinary mining?

Traditional mining rewards miners for solving arbitrary hashing. Proof-of-Useful-Work (PoUW) attempts to replace those tasks with computation that has value outside the network.

Ambient is building an L1 where miners also act as AI inference providers.

Users submit jobs through an onchain auction where miners bid to process them. The winner returns the output and commits to the logits produced during inference. Selected validators verify that the claimed inference was performed correctly.

The proposed model turns verified AI work into an accumulated measure of validated work called Logit Stake. Miners with higher LStake have greater influence in future leader selection.

Customer requests originate through the network’s auction, making externally demanded inference distinguishable from network-generated work used to absorb excess capacity.

Ambient could secure its blockchain with AI work that customers want completed.

It’s easy to hold grace when things are going well; the question is whether you can you keep your commitment during times of stress 

This is the core premise of Parshah Vayelech. 

We recount the last of Moshes life in our reading this week. In his final speech to Israelites he outlines a path forward: 

“I have set before you life and goodness, and death and evil: in that I command you this day to love G‑d, to walk in His ways and to keep His commandments��. . . Life and death I have set before you, blessing and curse. And you shall choose life.”

Every day we are faced with a choice — will we act with honor? Will we uphold the covenant?

To walk the righteous path requires us to critically examine the actions we take. An unconscious life is not a life of virtue. 

We end with the prediction that the Israelites will turn away from God at a certain point. At a low; a time of stress. 

This is natural. It is the human response. Something bad has happened, therefore I recoil from the path I am on.

It’s this instinct we must avoid. The instinct to criticize, to degrade simply because it is hard for you in the moment.

Breathe, move past, and recommit to the values that stood the test of time. 

This is something that I struggle with as well — no one is perfect. Remember that tomorrow is a new day, and at any moment you can choose to be better. 

Shabbat Shalom

$ZIM - Are You Long Enough? 

A very important article for understanding market behavior:

https://t.co/TtiXYjDv7A

The supply of new vessels has increased by 6.5% annually over the past five and a half years.

Almost no vessels have been scrapped. Only 300,000 TEU, less than 1% of the fleet, was scrapped during this period. Under normal conditions, at least 11% should have been scrapped.

Supply grew by approximately 5% more than average demand each year, yet the shortage only became more severe.

Approximately 15% of the fleet is more than 20 years old, historically the point at which vessels are scrapped.

The Suez Canal is beginning to reopen. More than 50% of the traffic has already returned and has been absorbed by the shortage. A full reopening is expected to release another 3%–4% of capacity, which we believe will also be absorbed relatively easily.

Conclusions:

Our theory is that the need for vessels is significantly higher than the historical average of 5%. Our estimate it is closer to 8% annually because growth is not evenly distributed, requiring more vessels on the routes where demand is concentrated.

Port congestion continues to worsen, creating a need for even more vessels.
The physical market correctly understood the real demand for capacity, despite what the “smart” analysts were saying. Those who listened to them paid a heavy price. 

Hapag-Lloyd and Maersk are managed by bureaucrats rather than businesspeople capable of conducting their own independent analysis.

We are probably approaching a golden age for shipping. Every available bit of capacity has been absorbed, and there is nowhere left to find additional vessels. The industry must begin scrapping more ships.

P.S. Notice that ZIM’s vessels chartered under long-term agreements are effectively owned by the company.

Here is why: ZIM has an option to purchase them at the end of the charter period at a bargain price, say approximately $20 million per vessel. Discounted to today, with roughly 12 years remaining, the present value of that purchase option is only around $5–7 million per vessel.

Therefore, these vessels can effectively be treated as owned. And if an unforeseen catastrophe occurs, the right not to exercise the purchase option would itself be worth several million dollars, meaning the effective exercise price is close to zero.
